title: More than one
goal: Form plurals using the five patterns Swedish has — and learn to tell which pattern a noun belongs to before you ever memorize it word by word.
bekal: the five plural groups and the clue that gives each one away
talk about your family members and ask about someone else's family

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Familjen på telefonen
dialogs.intro: Sunday afternoon. Elin walks into the kitchen and finds Dian just ending a video call, a family photo still open in front of her.

lines.speaker: Elin:
lines.id: Who are the people in the picture?

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Det är min familj. Vi är sex personer.
lines.id: That's my family. There are six of us.
lines.literal: it is my family. we are six persons.

lines.speaker: Elin:
lines.id: Six! Do you have brothers and sisters?

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Ja, jag har två bröder och en syster. Bröderna bor kvar hemma.
lines.id: Yes, I have two brothers and a sister. My brothers still live at home.
lines.literal: yes, I have two brothers and a sister. brothers-the live remaining at-home.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Hon är lärare. Hon har trettio elever i klassen.
lines.id: She's a teacher. She has thirty students in her class.
lines.literal: she is teacher. she has thirty pupils in class-the.

lines.speaker: Elin:
lines.text: Trettio barn! Här har vi bara tjugo i varje klass.
lines.id: Thirty kids! Here we only have twenty in each class.
lines.literal: thirty children! here have we only twenty in every class.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.id: Do you have a big family?

lines.speaker: Elin:
lines.text: Nej, vi är tre. Men vi har fyra katter och två hundar.
lines.id: No, there are three of us. But we have four cats and two dogs.
lines.literal: no, we are three. but we have four cats and two dogs.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.id: So the animals are family too!

lines.speaker: Elin:
lines.text: Precis. Fråga mina föräldrar — de säger samma sak.
lines.id: Exactly. Ask my parents — they'll tell you the same thing.
lines.literal: exactly. ask my parents — they say same thing.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Jag saknar mina föräldrar. Men vi hörs varje söndag.
lines.id: I miss my parents. But we talk every Sunday.
lines.literal: I miss my parents. but we hear-each-other every Sunday.

notes: **Syskon** means "siblings" with no gender attached — one everyday word for "brothers and sisters". English has *sibling*, but it sounds formal; in Swedish *syskon* is the normal, spoken word. The plural looks exactly like the singular (*ett syskon* → *syskon*), so *har du syskon?* already means "do you have any brothers or sisters?".

**Like English, Swedish doesn't split siblings by age.** *En bror* is a brother of any age; *en syster* a sister. When age really matters, you add an adjective: *storebror* (big brother), *lillasyster* (little sister) — just like English "big brother" and "little sister".

**Bröder, not brorar.** A handful of very common nouns change their vowel in the plural: *en bror* → *bröder*, *en bok* → *böcker*, *en man* → *män*, *en fot* → *fötter*. There are only about two dozen of them, and almost all are words you'll use every day, so they stick through use, not through lists. English does the very same thing: *man* → *men*, *foot* → *feet*.

**Vilka** is the plural of *vilken/vilket* ("which"). When asking about several people at once, Swedes say *vilka är det?* ("who are they?"), not *vem är det?*. If you're asking about just one person: *vem är det?*

**Föräldrar** (parents) almost always appears in the plural; the singular *en förälder* ("a parent") exists but is used far less — mostly in official contexts, much as English "a parent" is less common than "my parents".

**Vi hörs** — "talk soon", literally "we hear each other". Together with *vi ses* ("see you"), it's the most common way to sign off a phone call. Both use the *-s* ending, which makes the verb mutual: "each other".

grammars.title: The five plural groups
body: Every Swedish noun falls into one of these five groups. The "clue" column is the part worth keeping — it predicts the right group for most words.

head: Group
Ending
Example
Clue
rows: en stol → stol**ar** · en pojke → pojk**ar**
en bok → böck**er** · en student → student**er**
*en*-loanwords (stress at the end) & some one-syllable words
ett hus → hus · ett barn → barn

after: Group 5 is the good news textbooks rarely shout about: **every *ett*-word ending in a consonant stays exactly the same in the plural**. *Ett hus* → *hus*, *ett barn* → *barn*, *ett rum* → *rum*, *ett kök* → *kök*. The number tells you how many: *tre hus*, *fem barn* — just like English *one sheep, five sheep*.

Group 3 often changes the vowel inside the word too (*bok* → *böcker*, *hand* → *händer*, *natt* → *nätter*). It's a leftover from old Germanic, and English kept exactly the same leftover: *foot* → *feet*, *man* → *men*, *goose* → *geese*.
Newer English loanwords usually go into group 3: *en dator* → *datorer*, *en film* → *filmer*, *en app* → *appar* (that one is group 2, because it has one syllable).

grammars.title: The definite plural: "the + many"
body: Once the plural is formed, the definite ending is added on top. Which ending you add depends on the **gender of the word**, not on its plural group.
after: The rule fits into one sentence: **if the plural ends in a consonant (-r, -n), add *-na* or *-a*; if the plural doesn't change at all, add *-en*.**

Notice that *husen* is "the houses" while *huset* is "the house". One letter apart, and it's the only spot in all of Swedish grammar where singular and plural are easy to mix up. Read the endings carefully.

blocks.text: Swedish names grandparents with wonderful precision: **mormor** = "mother's mother", **farmor** = "father's mother", **morfar** = "mother's father", **farfar** = "father's father". Where English just says "grandma" and leaves you guessing which side, Swedish tells you. Once you see the pattern, there's nothing left to memorize. It carries on to aunts and uncles: **morbror** (uncle on your mother's side), **faster** (aunt on your father's side, from *far* + *syster*).

blocks.title: Asking about family
items: **Har du syskon?** — Do you have any brothers or sisters?
**Hur många är ni i familjen?** — How many are there in your family?
**Var bor dina föräldrar?** — Where do your parents live?
**Jag är enda barnet.** — I'm an only child.
**Jag saknar min familj.** — I miss my family.

sections.title: Counting things, and a word called sak

blocks.text: A number in front of a noun is always followed by the **indefinite plural** — no *en/ett*, no definite ending. *Tre böcker*, *fem hus*, *tjugo elever*.

head: Wrong
Right
Why
rows: no definite form after a number
*mycket* is for things you can't count

blocks.text: **Många** is used for things you can count (books, people, days), **mycket** for things you can't (coffee, water, time, money). Good news: this is exactly the English split between *many* and *much* — *many books*, *much coffee*. The only difference is that Swedes use *mycket* all the time in positive sentences too, where English would say "a lot of": *Han har mycket pengar* = "He has a lot of money".

blocks.title: En sak, ett ting, en grej
items: **En sak** — "thing, matter". The most useful word when you've forgotten what something is called: *Vad heter den där saken?*
**En grej** — the casual version, a bit like "thingy" or "stuff" in conversation. *Ge mig den där grejen.*
**Samma sak** — "the same thing". *De säger samma sak.*
**Grejen är att…** — "the thing is…", a sentence opener young Swedes use constantly.
